title: THE “SONS OF GOD” SAW THAT HUMAN WOMEN WERE BEAUTIFUL AND TOOK WIVES—WHO WERE THESE MYSTERIOUS MEN?
paragraphs: THE “SONS OF GOD” SAW THAT HUMAN WOMEN WERE BEAUTIFUL AND TOOK WIVES—WHO WERE THESE MYSTERIOUS MEN?

Genesis 6 contains four of the strangest verses in the Bible. But what if our obsession with the mysterious “sons of God” has caused us to miss the terrifying warning—and the breathtaking grace—standing right beside them?
There are passages in Scripture that comfort you.
There are passages that correct you.
And then there are passages that make you stop reading, move your eyes back to the beginning of the sentence, and whisper…
“Wait. What did I just read?”
Genesis 6:1–4 is one of those passages.
Humanity is multiplying. Daughters are being born. Civilization is expanding.
Then, without warning, the biblical narrative gives us one of the most mysterious statements in the Old Testament:
וַיִּרְאוּ בְנֵי־הָאֱלֹהִים אֶת־בְּנוֹת הָאָדָם כִּי טֹבֹת הֵנָּה
Vayyir'u bene-ha'elohim et-benot ha'adam ki tovot hennah.
In straightforward English:

“The sons of God saw the daughters of man, that they were good/beautiful…”
—Genesis 6:2
And then:
וַיִּקְחוּ לָהֶם נָשִׁים מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּחָרוּ
Vayyiqchu lahem nashim mikkol asher bacharu.
“…and they took for themselves women/wives from whomever they chose.”
Who were these “sons of God”?
Angels?
Fallen heavenly beings?
Powerful human rulers?
Descendants of Seth?
And what in the world were the Nephilim?
Giants?
Warriors?
Hybrid offspring?
Ancient tyrants whose reputations became legendary?
Those questions have fascinated readers for centuries.
But before chasing giants, angels, bloodlines, ancient legends, or sensational theories, we need to do something much less exciting—and much more important.
We need to listen to what the Bible actually says.
The Hebrew expression translated “sons of God” is:
בְנֵי־הָאֱלֹהִים — bene ha'elohim.
Bene means “sons of,” while ha'elohim contains the familiar word Elohim.
The expression itself is real.
The mystery surrounding its precise identification is also real.
And Christians should be careful not to transform biblical mystery into dogmatic certainty where Scripture itself has not given us that certainty.
One ancient interpretation understands these “sons of God” as heavenly beings.
That interpretation did not originate with modern conspiracy videos.
Similar “sons of God” language elsewhere in the Old Testament can describe members of the heavenly assembly. Job 1:6, for example, describes the bene ha'elohim presenting themselves before the LORD.
That makes the heavenly-being interpretation a serious reading rather than something we should simply laugh away.
Ancient Jewish interpretation also developed the idea of rebellious heavenly beings associated with the events surrounding Genesis 6. Later Jewish writings expanded that tradition dramatically.
Some Christians also connect Genesis 6 with passages such as Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4, which speak of angels who sinned and were judged.
Yet caution is necessary.
Genesis 6 itself never stops and says:
“By sons of God, Moses means fallen angels.”
That explanatory sentence simply isn't there.

And Jesus taught that angels in heaven “neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30). Christians differ over how directly that statement should be applied to Genesis 6, particularly because Jesus specifically speaks about angels in heaven.
So the heavenly-being interpretation has ancient roots and textual arguments behind it—but questions remain.
There is another historic interpretation.
Some readers understand the “sons of God” as powerful rulers, nobles, judges, or warrior-kings who abused their position.
That possibility becomes especially interesting when you slow down over the verbs.
They saw.
They desired.
They took.
From whomever they chose.
There is something chilling about that sequence.
Beauty was observed.
Desire awakened.
Power reached out.
And women were taken.
Whatever else Genesis 6:2 means, this is hardly presented as a beautiful biblical romance.
It sounds disturbingly like a world in which those possessing power believed desire gave them permission.
And suddenly this strange ancient passage doesn't feel quite so ancient anymore.
How much human evil has begun with the same lie?
“I want it, therefore I deserve it.”
“I can take it, therefore I am allowed to have it.”
“I have power, therefore nobody can tell me no.”
That spirit has destroyed marriages.
It has corrupted ministries.
It has exploited women.
It has destroyed men.
It has poisoned businesses.
It has turned authority into domination.
It has transformed blessing into entitlement.
And it has whispered to countless human hearts:
If you want it badly enough, take it.
Genesis knows that voice.
It has heard it before.
Eve saw that the tree was good.
She took its fruit.
Genesis 6 tells us that the sons of God saw the daughters of humanity were desirable.
And they took.
See.
Desire.
Take.
The vocabulary should make us uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the greatest monster hiding in Genesis 6 isn't a giant.
Perhaps it is uncontrolled desire.

There is also a third major interpretation Christians have held: that the “sons of God” represent the godly line associated with Seth while the “daughters of man” represent women from an ungodly human line, often associated with Cain.

On this reading, Genesis describes the collapse of spiritual separation as people belonging to a covenant-conscious lineage abandon faithfulness and choose relationships according to outward attraction rather than devotion to God.
This interpretation became especially influential within portions of Christian tradition.
Yet it also faces questions because Genesis 6 does not explicitly call the men “sons of Seth” or explicitly identify the women as “daughters of Cain.”
Again…
Humility.
Sometimes faithfulness to Scripture means refusing to say more than Scripture says.
The Bible does not become less authoritative because we admit that one difficult passage is difficult.
Quite the opposite.
We honor Scripture when we allow Scripture to speak in its own words instead of forcing it to say whatever makes our theory work.
Then Genesis introduces another famous word:
הַנְּפִלִים — ha-Nephilim.
“The Nephilim.”
Genesis 6:4 says:
הַנְּפִלִים הָיוּ בָאָרֶץ בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם
Ha-nephilim hayu va'aretz bayyamim hahem.
“The Nephilim were on the earth in those days…”
The exact derivation and meaning of Nephilim have been debated for centuries.
It is commonly connected with the Hebrew root n-f-l, associated with “falling,” although proposed explanations of the name differ.
And notice something people often overlook.
Genesis does not give us a detailed anatomy lesson.
It doesn't tell us their exact height.
It doesn't give us their skeletal measurements.
It doesn't provide a chart explaining supernatural genetics.
Instead it continues:
הֵמָּה הַגִּבֹּרִים אֲשֶׁר מֵעוֹלָם אַנְשֵׁי הַשֵּׁם
Hemmah haggibborim asher me'olam anshei hashem.
They were the gibborim—the mighty ones, warriors, powerful men of ancient times—“men of the name,” commonly rendered “men of renown.”
And there is an irony here that is almost painful.
They had a name.
They had reputation.
They had power.
They had renown.
People knew who they were.
Perhaps people feared them.
Perhaps people celebrated them.
Perhaps mothers told stories about them.
Perhaps generations remembered their exploits.
They were the celebrities of a dying world.
And none of their fame could save them.
Read that again.
They were famous in a world God was about to judge.
That sentence should haunt us.
Because we live in a civilization obsessed with becoming anshei hashem—people of the name.
We want followers.
Recognition.
Influence.
Status.
Verification.
Applause.
People knowing who we are.
Even Christians can secretly become intoxicated by being known.
We can build platforms while neglecting prayer.
We can defend reputations while hiding sin.
We can learn how to appear spiritual without becoming holy.
We can make our names recognizable while the name of Jesus becomes increasingly decorative in our lives.
And Genesis whispers from the ruins of the ancient world:
Being known by everybody means nothing if you are not walking with God.
Because immediately after this strange account comes the sentence that explains the spiritual condition of the world.
Genesis 6:5:
וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי רַבָּה רָעַת הָאָדָם בָּאָרֶץ
Vayyar YHWH ki rabbah ra'at ha'adam ba'aretz.
“The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth…”
Notice the repeated idea.
They saw.
And God saw.
Humanity saw what it desired.
God saw what humanity had become.
They looked outward and saw beauty to possess.
God looked inward and saw hearts corrupted by evil.
That is where Genesis 6 becomes frighteningly personal.
Because you and I can control what people see.
God sees what people never see.
He sees the browser history nobody knows about.
He sees the private resentment beneath the worship song.
He sees the jealousy hidden underneath congratulations.
He sees the secret conversation.
The compromise.
The fantasy.
The bitterness.
The addiction.
The pride disguised as ministry.
The hunger for applause disguised as “influence.”
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Him.
The thing you keep deleting.
The thing you keep returning to.
The thing you promised Jesus you would surrender.
People see the profile.
God sees the heart.
And perhaps that is why this story bothers us.
We came looking for mysterious beings.
Scripture turned the mirror toward us.
We wanted to ask:
“Who were the sons of God?”
God may be asking:
“What are you becoming?”
Because the ultimate story of Genesis 6 is not merely about mysterious beings.
It is about a world collapsing beneath the weight of rebellion.
Humanity had multiplied technologically, socially, culturally, and physically…
while deteriorating spiritually.
And then comes judgment.
The Flood.
The undoing of a corrupted world.
Sin is not harmless.
God's patience should never be confused with God's approval.
The God of Scripture is holy.
He sees exploitation.
He sees violence.
He sees sexual corruption.
He sees injustice.
He sees what powerful people do when nobody can stop them.
And He sees what ordinary people hide when nobody is watching.
But if Genesis 6 ended only with human corruption, we would have reason to despair.
It doesn't.
Hidden near the approaching storm is one of the most beautiful sentences in Genesis.
וְנֹחַ מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה
Ve-Noach matza chen be'einei YHWH.

“But Noah found favor/grace in the eyes of the LORD.”
—Genesis 6:8
There it is.
חֵן — chen.
Favor.
Grace.
Human wickedness was great.
But grace was still there.
Judgment was approaching.
But grace was still there.
Civilization was corrupt.
But grace was still there.
The famous had their names.
The mighty had their strength.
The powerful took what they wanted.
But one man's story became marked by something infinitely greater.
Grace.
And now the entire mystery begins pointing beyond Noah.
Because Noah's ark could preserve human life through water…
but Noah could not cure the human heart.
The Flood judged a wicked generation.
It did not remove sin from human nature.
Humanity needed something greater than an ark.
We needed a Savior.
And eventually another Son would enter humanity's darkness.
Not a mysterious “son of God” taking whatever pleased Him.
The eternal Son of God giving Himself for sinners who had nothing worthy to offer Him.
Jesus did not come to exploit humanity.
He came to rescue humanity.
He did not come demanding that sinners bleed for Him.
He bled for sinners.
He did not come merely to condemn the guilty from a safe distance.
He stepped into our judgment.
The cross tells the truth Genesis 6 already forces us to confront:
Sin is worse than we imagine.
And grace is greater than we deserve.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ carried the judgment our rebellion deserved.
The innocent One stood where the guilty should have stood.
The Holy One was numbered with transgressors.
The One with the greatest Name humbled Himself.
The King wore thorns.
The Creator was nailed to wood.
The Son of God entered death…
and three days later walked out of the grave.
That is the Gospel.
Not “become good enough and maybe God will accept you.”
Not “hide your scandal carefully enough and religious people will respect you.”
Not “build such a powerful name that nobody remembers your failures.”
No.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Trust Jesus Christ.
Receive the mercy you cannot purchase.
Let Him begin changing what sin has distorted.
Maybe your scandal isn't Genesis 6.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe you have spent years carefully managing appearances.
Maybe your marriage is hurting.
Maybe pornography has become your secret prison.
Maybe bitterness has lived inside you so long that it feels like personality.
Maybe you have wandered from Christ while still posting Christian verses.
Maybe you know exactly how to sound saved while privately wondering how far your heart has gone.
Then hear this.
Your sin matters.
Repentance matters.
Judgment is real.
But your story does not have to end where your sin wrote its darkest sentence.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Jesus still forgives the repentant.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still breaks chains.
Jesus still receives prodigals.
Jesus still turns graves into testimonies.
Jesus still rewrites stories.
That is why our message will always be:
Not because scandal doesn't matter.
But because scandal does not have the final word when Jesus Christ takes hold of a surrendered life.
So maybe the question you need to answer tonight isn't whether the sons of God were angels, rulers, or descendants of Seth.
Study that question.
Search the Scriptures.
Think carefully.
Hold your conclusions with biblical conviction and appropriate humility.
But don't become so fascinated with the identity of the Nephilim that you ignore the condition of your own heart.
The ancient world had mighty men.
God looked for righteousness.
The ancient world celebrated names.
God looked at hearts.
The ancient world followed desire.
God called humanity to account.
And somewhere tonight, perhaps while reading these words, somebody knows that God has just touched the place they have been trying hardest to hide.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Ask for help if you need help.
Come home.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, you don't have to explain your whole story publicly.

And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another wounded person from giving up tonight.
Not because every difficult question in Genesis 6 has been solved in a few paragraphs.
“See it. Want it. Take it.”
And you may need to remember that God sees farther than desire does.
Not merely to help an algorithm.
And yes—even send it privately to the person who would never call themselves a Christian but keeps asking questions about the Bible.
One share can open a conversation.
One conversation can lead someone back to Scripture.
And God can use Scripture to lead a sinner to Christ.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.
And not because anyone should give under spiritual pressure.
Scripture teaches, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Christian generosity is worship when it rises freely from a heart grateful to God.
But the greatest reason to stay connected isn't merchandise.
It's growth.
It's being sharpened.
Convicted.
Encouraged.
Corrected.
Comforted.
Pointed repeatedly toward Jesus Christ.
Jesus Christ is worth following.
Your eternity is worth taking seriously.
Your hidden life is worth surrendering.
Your Bible is worth opening.
Your family is worth praying for.
Your sin is worth confessing.
The Gospel is worth sharing.
And the grace of Christ is greater than the version of you that you are ashamed for anyone else to meet.
Save what strengthens you.
Share what somebody else needs.
And comment—not for empty engagement, but because sometimes saying “Jesus, I need You” in front of others becomes the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
The “sons of God” in Genesis 6 may remain one of Scripture's most debated mysteries.
But the most important truth in the chapter isn't mysterious at all.
Humanity falls.
God sees.
Sin brings judgment.
Grace appears.
And ultimately…
Christ comes.
The ancient mighty men became memories.
The men of renown lost their world.
But the name above every name remains.
Jesus.
And when the last secret has been exposed, the last reputation has faded, and every human name has been stripped of its earthly applause, that is the Name that will still matter.
Your darkest chapter does not have to become your final chapter when the pen is surrendered to Jesus.
